title: Why GPUs Power Deep Learning
hook: Neural networks are parallel by nature, and a GPU runs thousands of threads at once - so the same math that crawls on a CPU maps naturally onto a GPU and trains far faster.
key_points: Neural networks are highly parallel, and a GPU has hundreds of cores running thousands of threads simultaneously.
That parallelism maps the math of training onto GPUs, giving a large speedup over CPU-only training.
Training a deep network adjusts millions to billions of parameters via backpropagation.
Common frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow target GPUs out of the box.
content_html: If you have ever wondered why deep learning and GPUs are practically synonymous, NVIDIA's explainer gives the short answer: the work neural networks do is naturally parallel, and GPUs are built to do many things at once. It is a good first stop before diving into the harder hardware details.
extra_html:
How it works

Neural networks are highly parallel by nature - the same kind of math repeated across many units at the same time. A GPU has hundreds of cores that run thousands of threads simultaneously, so that math maps directly onto the chip instead of being squeezed through a handful of CPU cores one piece at a time. The result is a large speedup over CPU-only training. The training itself works by adjusting millions to billions of parameters through backpropagation, and that is exactly the repeated, parallel arithmetic GPUs excel at.

Why it matters

This is why GPUs became the default workhorse for deep learning, and why common frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow target them directly so you rarely have to think about the underlying parallelism. For a beginner-friendly walkthrough of the terms, the NVIDIA explainer is the place to read more.

related.hook: Google built a custom chip whose heart is a 256x256 grid of 8-bit multiply-accumulate units - and in production it ran neural-net inference roughly 15-30x faster than the GPUs and CPUs of its day.
